study_identification_part.si4_title: Investigating dopaminergic abnormalities in schizophrenia and first-episode psychosis with normative modelling and multisite molecular neuroimaging

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: Apply normative modelling (NM) to dopaminergic PET ([11C]-(+)-PHNO and [18F]FDOPA) to build healthy-control reference distributions and quantify individual deviations in psychosis, evaluating scanner/site harmonization and clinical utility (e.g., treatment response).

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: The study compared Gaussian kernel smoothing and ComBat harmonization. ComBat was chosen as the optimal method and applied to both [11C]-(+)-PHNO and [18F]FDOPA data. ComBat was used to adjust for scanner effects, preserving age, sex, and BMI (for PHNO) as covariates.
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: To harmonise the [11C]-(+)-PHNO scans we employed two methods widely used in the literature: Gaussian kernel smoothing [38] and Combat harmonisation [36, 37]... Combat returned the smallest differences, hence better harmonisation performances... Based on the outcome of this analysis of performance, we then used the identi /uniFB01 ed method to harmonise the [ 18 F]FDOPA datasets before the NM step.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Psychosis cohorts show substantially higher and spatially heterogeneous FDOPA deviations than controls (~2–3x more extreme voxels), with limited overlap across patients (<~20%); harmonization via ComBat effectively mitigates scanner/site effects; striatal FDOPA deviations predict treatment response (AUC ~0.77–0.83).
